compiledFrom: FETCHER ledger of 20 sources (S1–S20) + 11 attemptedAndFailed items. No source outside that ledger is cited anywhere in this file. Every entry, variant, goldenValue and contested point carries at least one sid.
system: Chinese shichen 時辰 — twelve double-hours named for the twelve earthly branches (地支) 子丑寅卯辰巳午未申酉戌亥, each a fixed division of the whole day-and-night rather than of daylight, carrying (a) a descriptive day-part name (半夜, 雞鳴, 平旦 …), (b) an animal paired with the same branch in the Lunheng, (c) a 刻 (ke) subdivision layer whose count per day moved between 100, 120, 108 and 96, and (d) a later almanac hour-selection layer. NO RULER COLUMN: no snippet in the ledger assigns a planet, deity or presiding figure to any shichen, and the maintainer's grid ruling places shichen among the four systems that must not render one.
rulerColumnJustification: FALSE on two independent grounds, and the ruler property is omitted from every entry rather than filled with 'none'. (1) MAINTAINER'S GRID RULING (binding): of six systems only Vedic horā has a Tier A ruler column and only Choghadiya a Tier C one; shichen, zmanim, Egyptian and Babylonian have none and must not render one. (2) THE LEDGER SUPPLIES NOTHING TO FILL IT: across all 20 sources and 96 snippets, not one assigns a planet, deity or presiding figure to a shichen. What the ledger DOES attach to a branch is an animal (S14-a…S14-h, S16-a, S16-b), a descriptive day-part name (S15-a, S15-b, S9-a…S9-c), a ke allotment (S1-l, S10-a, S10-b, S10-c, S12-a) and — in the hemerological layer only — a conditional auspiciousness that is a function of the DAY's branch, not a property of the hour (S13-e, S13-f). NOTE THE LIMIT ON GROUND (2): the fetcher states plainly that it did not search for a ruler and makes no absence claim. This dossier therefore records the ruler question as could-not-determine in gaps[], not as a confirmed gap. The column is empty because the maintainer ruled it empty and because nothing retrieved fills it — not because anyone has demonstrated that no Chinese source anywhere assigns one.
dayStart: 23:00 CIVIL CLOCK, at the START of 子時 — with two attested departures kept unresolved beside it. THE MAINSTREAM POSITION: the first double-hour begins at 23 hr local time (S3-a, Tier B), so the twelve run 23:00→01:00→03:00→…→21:00→23:00; the practitioner and tertiary sources agree (S17-b, S18-a, Tier C). This is not merely a modern convention read back: the 1741 imperial 協紀辨方書 states that 子正初刻 falls at the MIDDLE of 子 and 午正初刻 at the middle of 午 (S13-a, Tier A), which places midnight at zi's midpoint and therefore zi's start an hour before it; and the 清史稿 reckons a calendrical epoch 從…己卯日子正為始, from 子正 (S6-b, Tier A). DEPARTURE 1 — THE SONG: Sôma, Kawabata & Tanikawa (2004) report that in the Song the first double-hour began at 0 hr local time, so zi ran 00:00–02:00 with midnight at its beginning (S3-b, S3-m); the tertiary summary says the same (S17-b). DEPARTURE 2 — 夜子時 / early-zi vs late-zi: the 1715 御定月令輯要 records a construct in which 夜子 falls after 亥時 and so has only an 初刻 and no 正刻, while 子時 has only a 正刻 and no 初刻 (S10-h, Tier A) — i.e. the zi block is split across the day boundary; a modern commercial practitioner page states the same split as two rival schools, one changing the day at 23:00 and one at 00:00 (S18-c, S18-d, Tier C). A THIRD, UNRELATED DAY-START SITS IN THE SAME LEDGER AND MUST NOT BE MERGED: the 明史 records that the HUIHUI (Islamic) method starts the day at 午正, with 午初四刻 belonging to the previous day (S7-b) — that is the Islamic astronomical method as recorded in a Chinese official history, not the Chinese civil shichen day, and the fetcher flags it as such.
divisionRule: TWELVE EQUAL FIXED DIVISIONS OF THE WHOLE NYCHTHEMERON, NOT OF DAYLIGHT. The day is divided into 12 double-hours (S3-a); each Chinese hour makes up two Western hours (S19-a, Tier C); they are named for the earthly branches in order (S17-a, Tier C) and that order is the fixed branch sequence given by the Tier A day-part lists (S15-a, S15-b). THE STRUCTURAL PROOF IS ARITHMETICAL AND IT IS TIER A: the 隋書 records that in Liang 天監 6 (AD 507) Emperor Wu found 晝夜百刻，分配十二辰，辰得八刻，仍有餘分 — a hundred ke of day-and-night distributed over twelve chen give each chen eight ke with a remainder — and so reformed the day to 乃以晝夜為九十六刻，一辰有全刻八焉 (S1-f, S1-g; independently confirmed in the Siku transcript S2-b, S2-c). A scheme that distributes a FIXED daily total evenly over twelve chen is by construction a scheme of equal fixed divisions. The 明史 states the same priority from the other side: 命日為九十六刻，使每時得八刻無奇零 — the day was made 96 ke SO THAT each shi gets eight ke without remainder (S5-a). The shi is the invariant; the ke was refitted to it, twice. SUBDIVISION: each double-hour is halved into 初 (initial) and 正 (central) (S17-c, Tier C; S3-h, Tier B, on the Yuanshi system), and the halving is visible in Tier A usage throughout — 子正, 午正, 辰正, 申正, 巳正, 午初二刻 (S13-a, S13-c, S1-k, S4-d, S8-f). Below that sits the ke: under the 100-ke day one shichen is 8⅓ ke (S3-e, Tier B; 八刻六十分刻之二十為一時 in the 五代史 memorial quoted by Gu Yanwu, S8-e; 每八刻二十分為一時 in the 漏刻經 quoted by the 御定月令輯要, S10-a); under the 96-ke day one shichen is exactly 8 ke of 15 minutes (S5-a, S6-a; S17-e, Tier C). WHAT IS SEASONAL IS A DIFFERENT LAYER: the 隋書 varies the SPLIT of the fixed total between daylight and darkness — 冬至晝漏四十刻，夜漏六十刻 (S1-b), 春秋二分，晝夜各五十刻 (S1-c) — and Yuan Chong's AD 594 submission tabulates 冬至：日出辰正，入申正，晝四十刻，夜六十刻 (S1-k, S2-e). The chen themselves do not lengthen or shorten. DERIVED CLOCK RANGES, LABELLED AS SUCH: only two branches carry a clock range read off a retrieved page — 子 at 23 hr (S3-a; S18-a) and 午 at 11–13 hr (S3-k; S18-b). The other ten ranges in this dossier are the COMPILER'S ARITHMETIC on three attested premises (twelve equal double-hours S3-a/S19-a · fixed branch order S17-a/S15-a/S15-b · zi anchored at 23:00 S3-a), and they are carried in a separate field name, clockRangeDerived, so that no renderer can show them as something a source stated. The two attested anchors are mutually consistent with the derivation, which is the only check on it this ledger permits.
polarBehaviour: NO POLAR FAILURE MODE, and the absence is the finding. The twelve chen are defined by a fixed count of equal divisions of the civil day (S3-a, S19-a) anchored on a clock instant (S3-a; S13-a places 子正初刻 at zi's midpoint; S6-b reckons an epoch from 子正), with no term in any retrieved statement of the rule that refers to sunrise, sunset or altitude. A system so defined is a total function of the civil timestamp: it is as well formed above the Arctic Circle in December as it is at the Sui capital in March, and a comparison view must NOT route shichen through the repo's seasonal-hour machinery. THE SOLAR-DEPENDENT LAYERS ARE ADJACENT AND SEPARATE, and those would degenerate: the daylight/darkness split of the fixed ke total (S1-b winter solstice 40/60, S1-c equinoxes 50/50), Yuan Chong's tabulated sunrise and sunset chen (S1-k, S2-e), and his shadow instrument that divides the twelve chen evenly and reads the chen off where the sun's shadow points (S2-h) — an instrument that has nothing to point at during polar night. ONE LONGITUDE CAVEAT, TIER C AND REPORTED WITHOUT EXTENSION: a commercial practitioner page states that the whole country runs on Beijing time as a single zone (S20-a), that when the sun is overhead in Beijing it is about 80 minutes from its zenith over Kashgar (S20-b), and that the offset is 4 minutes per degree (S20-c). The fetcher records explicitly that the page does NOT state that this moves the 23:00 shichen boundary and gives no figure for hour-pillar error; this dossier therefore reports the three statements and does not chain them into a boundary shift. That chaining would be the compiler's claim, not the page's.

entries.name: zi
entries.quality: 半夜 / 夜半 — 'midnight', the day-part the branch names
entries.note: The only branch whose clock anchor is stated outright in a retrieved source: the first double-hour began at 23 hr local time (S3-a). The Tier A texts give the same shape structurally rather than numerically — 子正初刻 falls at the MIDDLE of 子 (S13-a), and a calendrical epoch is reckoned 從…子正為始 (S6-b) — so midnight sits at zi's midpoint and its start an hour earlier, which is why the descriptive name is 半夜 and not 'day-break'. Two departures are kept beside it and neither is resolved here: the Song reckoning that began zi at 0 hr (S3-b, S3-m; S17-b), and the 夜子 construct in which the block after 亥時 carries only an 初刻 while 子時 carries only a 正刻 (S10-h), which a modern practitioner page restates as two rival schools (S18-c, S18-d). On the ke layer zi is one of the two shi that the 'old law' gave ten ke rather than eight (S12-a), a scheme the 1715 compilation also lists among the rival distributions (S10-f) — while 王氏詩解 puts zi among the eight shi of eight ke each (S10-b).
entries.toxicFlag: CONDITIONAL, NOT INTRINSIC. The 1741 協紀辨方書 gives the rule 時破大凶：日支衝時支也，如子日午時之類 — 'hour-breaking, greatly inauspicious: the day branch clashes the hour branch, as in the wu hour on a zi day' (S13-f). The flag attaches to a day/hour PAIR; zi appears here as the day term of the single worked example. The ledger supplies no other branch pair, so none is inferred.

entries.name: wu
entries.quality: 日中 — 'sun at the middle', noon
entries.note: The second of the two branches whose clock range a retrieved source states outright: the double-hour wu corresponds to 11 through 13 hr (S3-k, Tier B), and a practitioner chart gives 11:00–13:00 (S18-b, Tier C). Those two agree with the derivation from the zi anchor, which is the only cross-check this ledger allows. THE CENTRING QUESTION LIVES ON THIS BRANCH: the 1741 imperial manual states 午正初刻當午中, the 正 point at the middle of 午 (S13-a), and its worked example runs 午初二刻至午正二刻屬午方 (S13-c); Gu Yanwu quotes a memorial of AD 938 saying the shi was anciently CENTRED at 4 ke 10 fen — 時以四刻十分為正此自古所用也 (S8-e) — and complaining that in his source's own day the practice had been lost, 午正 being taken as the START of the shi and so encroaching four ke ten fen into 未 (S8-f). Both positions are kept. On the ke layer wu is the second of the two shi the 古法 gave ten ke (S12-a; also listed among the rivals at S10-f). Sôma et al. anchor the Song shift on this branch: in the Songshi it is the beginning of wu, and therefore zi begins at 0 hr instead of 23 (S3-m).

It is also the branch against which the 夜子 construct is defined: 夜子正在亥時之後 — the night-zi comes AFTER 亥時 and therefore has an 初刻 but no 正刻 (S10-h), which is the classical form of the day-boundary split that a modern practitioner page states as two rival schools (S18-c, S18-d). Yuan Chong's winter-solstice row assigns 亥 two ke, the same figure as 子 and 丑 (S1-l, S2-f); recorded, not interpreted.

variants.label: The count of ke in a day: 100 → 120 → 100 → 96 → 108 → 100 → … → 96
variants.tier: A (Chinese histories) + B (Sôma et al. 2004) + C (tertiary summary)
sequence: BASELINE — 其法，總以百刻，分於晝夜: the method totals a hundred ke, divided between day and night (S1-a; Siku control S2-a). Sôma et al. put the same baseline as 100 equal parts of the midnight-to-midnight interval, subdivided by fen, 'from the legendary era' (S3-c, S3-d).

HAN, EMPEROR AI — 至哀帝時，又改用晝夜一百二十刻，尋亦寢廢: changed to 120 ke, and soon fell into disuse (S1-e). Sôma et al. report the same from Hanshu ch. 26, the change described as temporary (S3-i). Gu Yanwu compresses both later reforms into one line: 漢哀新莽以百二十刻為日，梁武以九十六刻為日 (S8-d).
LIANG 天監 6 = AD 507 — THE FIRST 96-KE DAY, six centuries before any Jesuit. 武帝以晝夜百刻，分配十二辰，辰得八刻，仍有餘分 … 乃以晝夜為九十六刻，一辰有全刻八焉 (S1-f, S1-g; Siku control S2-b, S2-c).
LIANG 大同 10 = AD 544 — 又改用一百八刻: changed again, to 108 ke (S1-h).
CHEN 天嘉 era — 亦命舍人硃史造漏，依古百刻為法: a return to the ancient hundred-ke standard (S1-i; the Siku transcript reads 朱史 for 硃史, S2-d).

THE LONG PLATEAU — Sôma et al.: the same system of units continued until AD 1628 except for very short exceptional periods, during which the count was 96, 108 or 120; after 1628 it became 96 (S3-f, S3-g). The tertiary summary restates this and adds that the modern ke is 15 minutes (S17-d, S17-e).
variants.note: The 507 reform and the seventeenth-century one are the SAME arithmetic reached twice: 100 does not divide by 12, 96 does. The ledger supplies both independently and this dossier keeps both rather than crediting either with priority.

variants.label: How the hundred ke were shared among twelve shi — at least five rival schemes, none reconciled
schemes: 子午 ten ke each, the rest eight — 古法子午時皆十刻餘皆八刻故百刻 (S12-a). Arithmetic: 2×10 + 10×8 = 100.
寅申巳亥 nine ke each, the rest eight — 一日一夜通計一百刻，每八刻二十分為一時，惟寅申巳亥有九刻, quoting the 漏刻經 (S10-a; the transcript prints 己亥 for 巳亥). Arithmetic: 4×9 + 8×8 = 100.

辰戌丑未 nine ke each, the other eight shi eight — 寅申巳亥子午卯酉之八時每時各占八刻則合而為六十四刻 … 辰戌丑未之四時每時各占九刻則合而為三十六刻, quoting 王氏詩解 (S10-b, S10-c). Arithmetic: 64 + 36 = 100. THIS IS THE DIRECT CONVERSE OF THE PRECEDING SCHEME — the same 1715 compilation prints both, one giving the extra ke to 寅申巳亥 and the other explicitly giving those four eight.
子午卯酉 nine ke each, and a 子午 ten-ke variant — 其他或以子午二時各得十刻者，或以子午卯酉各得九刻者 (S10-f), with 或以夜子時得四刻者 added and all of them dismissed: 皆非也 (S10-g).
趙緣督's large/small split — 將十二時各分八刻，計刻九十六刻為大刻, twelve shi of eight large ke = 96, with the residue carried as twenty fen of small ke per shi (S10-e).

GU YANWU'S RECONCILIATION, the cleanest statement in the ledger — 歴家有大刻有小刻 (S8-a); 正一正二正三正四謂之大刻，合一日計之得九十六刻 (S8-b); 為初初者十二，為正初者十二，又得四大刻，合前為百刻 (S8-c). Twelve 初初 plus twelve 正初 small ke make four large ke; 96 + 4 = 100.
variants.note: The 1715 compilation's own verdict on the whole question, quoting the 蠡海集: 百刻之説衆議紛紛莫有定論 — the discussions of the hundred ke are many and clamorous, and there is no settled conclusion (S10-d). Yu Yan had posed the same problem in the Yuan: 一日百刻，以十二時分之，每時八刻，十二時計九十六刻 … 餘四刻安在? — where are the remaining four? Some say scattered at the junctions of the twelve shi, some say they are the 甲丙庚壬 hours; he rejects both (S11-a, S11-b). And the 隋書 records that in practice the ke of the twelve chen did differ in amount, and differed before and after 時正 (S1-j). The 1748 imperial commentary is what closes the file: 今時憲書時皆八刻，故晝夜共九十六刻 — under the current Shixian almanac every shi has eight ke, so day and night total 96 (S12-b).

variants.label: The twelve animals attach to the BRANCH, and the ledger never attaches one to an HOUR
content: THE EARLIEST WITNESS IN THE LEDGER IS AN ARGUMENT, NOT A LIST. The Lunheng's 物勢 chapter introduces the animals inside a five-phase disputation — 寅、木也，其禽虎也。戌、土也，其禽犬也 (S14-a); 丑、未、亦土也，丑禽牛，未禽羊也 (S14-b); 亥、水也，其禽豕也。巳、火也，其禽虵也 (S14-c); 子亦水也，其禽鼠也。午亦火也，其禽馬也 (S14-d) — and then restates a run of them in the following paragraph: 午、馬也，子、鼠也，酉、雞也，卯、兔也 (S14-e); 亥、豕也，未、羊也，丑、牛也 (S14-f); 巳、虵也，申、猴也 (S14-g). Eleven branches are covered.

THE DRAGON IS THE EXCEPTION AND THE FETCHER FLAGS IT. 辰 is absent from the 物勢 run. The pairing 辰為龍 comes from a different chapter, 言毒, in a passage about direction: 辰為龍，巳為蛇，辰、巳之位在東南 (S14-h). Anyone building a 'the Lunheng gives the twelve animals' row is building something the 物勢 chapter does not contain.

THE NINETEENTH-CENTURY LIST. Doolittle states that each of the twelve earthly branches is regarded as denoting one of twelve animals (S16-a) and gives them in the order of the horary characters: rat, cow, tiger, rabbit, dragon, snake, horse, sheep, monkey, cock, dog, boar (S16-b). Tier C, and the order matches the branch order the Tier A day-part lists give (S15-a, S15-b).

AND WHAT DOOLITTLE ATTACHES THEM TO IS THE YEAR. A person is said to be born under a certain animal, or to 'belong' to one (S16-c) — a year statement, not an hour statement. Separately he explains that a stem+branch pair denotes the first year, month, day OR hour of its cycle (S16-d), which is a statement about the sexagenary pairing, not about animals.
variants.note: CONSEQUENCE, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS VARIANT EXISTS. Two facts are separately attested — branch↔animal (S14, S16-a, S16-b) and branch↔hour (S15-a, S15-b, S9-a…S9-c) — and chaining them into 'the hour of the rat' would be the compiler's inference, not a source's claim. No retrieved source labels a double-hour with an animal, and searches of Doolittle vol. II for 'hour of the rat', 'double hour', 'twelve hours', 'divisions of time' and 'watches' returned no hits. The animal therefore appears in each entry's associations as the animal a source pairs with THAT BRANCH, worded so, and the corresponding gap entry records the search.

variants.label: The Song reckoning: the first double-hour begins at 0 hr, not 23
variants.note: Sôma, Kawabata & Tanikawa (2004) state in their abstract that it is confirmed in the paper that in the Song the first double-hour began at 0 hr local time, against the 23 hr they give as the general rule (S3-b against S3-a); the body ties it to the reference point in the Songshi being the beginning of wu, so zi begins at 0 hr instead of 23 (S3-m). The tertiary summary says the same and dates the change to the Song, with midnight then falling at the beginning of the first shi rather than inside it (S17-b). Kept as a live variant, not folded into the mainstream row. Cite-only: S3 and S17-derived wording must not be reproduced verbatim on the site (S3 is in copyright; S17 is CC BY-SA and would require share-alike).

variants.label: 早子時 / 晚子時 — where the calendar day changes inside zi
variants.note: The classical form is structural, not schismatic: 夜子正在亥時之後，故只有初刻而無正刻 … 子時却只有正刻而無初刻 — the night-zi follows 亥時 and so has an 初刻 with no 正刻, while 子時 has a 正刻 with no 初刻 (S10-h, 1715). The modern commercial form states it as two schools — an early-zi school in which the day pillar flips at 23:00 and the whole 23:00–01:00 block belongs to the next day, and a late-zi school in which 00:00 is the true start of the day (S18-c, S18-d, Tier C, cite-only, and the fetcher notes the page's own gloss on the second school is internally confusing). Against both stands the Tier A convention that 子正 is the MIDDLE of zi (S13-a) and is used as a calendrical epoch point (S6-b).

variants.label: Is the shi centred on its 正 point, or begun at it?
variants.note: THE 初/正 HALVING IS THE STRUCTURE THE DISPUTE IS ABOUT: each double-hour is split into an 'initial' 初 and a 'central' 正 half (S17-c, Tier C), which Sôma et al. describe for the Yuanshi system as each double hour being subdivided into two single hours (S3-h, Tier B). CENTRED: 八刻六十分刻之二十為一時，時以四刻十分為正，此自古所用也 — a shi is 8 ke and 20/60 of a ke, and is 'made 正' at 4 ke 10 fen, which is what antiquity used (Gu Yanwu quoting the 五代史 memorial of Ma Chongji, AD 938; S8-e). The 1741 imperial manual agrees eight centuries later: 子正初刻當子中，午正初刻當午中 (S13-a), with the worked example 午初二刻至午正二刻屬午方 (S13-c). BEGUN: the same 938 memorial complains that the practice had already been lost — 今失其傳，以午正為時始，下侵未四刻十分而為午 (S8-f). Sôma et al. read the Suishu as having each double-hour begin with 0 ke 0 fen (S3-l) and wu run 11 through 13 hr (S3-k), which is the centred convention expressed as a range. Both positions are printed; neither is resolved. A separate Tier A datum on how the boundary was ANNOUNCED rather than defined: 每時八刻二十分，每刻一擊鼓，八鼓後進時牌，餘二十分為鷄唱 — a drum-stroke per ke, the hour-tablet advanced after the eighth, the residual twenty fen marked by the cock-crow signal (S8-g).

variants.label: The seventeenth-century 96-ke changeover: which date, and whose reform
positions: 1628 — Sôma et al.: after 1628 the number of ke in a day became 96 (S3-g); the tertiary summary follows them, dating the 1/96 definition from 1628 and giving the modern ke as 15 minutes (S17-e).

MING FRAME, NO DATE — the 明史 records 命日為九十六刻，使每時得八刻無奇零，以之布算制器，甚便也 inside the passage on the Jesuits' arrival under Shenzong (S5-a, S5-b): the reform is described as convenient for computation and instrument-making, with no adoption year given in the retrieved snippet.

XU GUANGQI'S WORKING ASSUMPTION — di Serego Alighieri & Corsi assume Xu Guangqi used the Western 96-ke division of 15 minutes rather than the classical 100 ke of 14.4 minutes (S4-a, S4-b, Tier B, cite-only).

QING, SCHALL — 曰改定時刻，定晝夜為九十六刻 stands as one item in Adam Schall von Bell's forty-two points of the new method (S6-a); by Kangxi 4 (1665) the same change is being recited against him: 每日百刻，新法改為九十六刻 (S6-c).
QING, VERBIEST, KANGXI 8–9 — after the observatory trial, 南懷仁九十六刻之法既合天象，自應頒用 (S6-d), and the deliberation closes 應自康熙九年為始，用九十六刻之曆 — from Kangxi 9 (1670), the 96-ke calendar (S6-e).
SETTLED STATE, 1748 — 今時憲書時皆八刻，故晝夜共九十六刻 (S12-b).
variants.note: THE LEDGER DOES NOT SUPPORT 1645, the date this repo's round-1 shichen dossier carried. Two dates are attested here — 1628 (S3-g, S17-e) and Kangxi 9 = 1670 (S6-e) — and they are not the same event: the first is a change in the count of ke, the second an imperial decision to promulgate the 96-ke calendar after a rival system had been tried at the observatory and after the change had been prosecuted as a charge in 1665 (S6-c). Both are printed; neither is chosen.

variants.label: The Huihui (Islamic) method in the 明史 — a 96-ke, 24-hour scheme that is NOT the civil shichen day
variants.note: 時二十四，每時六十分。刻九十六。每刻十五分。 — twenty-four hours of sixty minutes each; ninety-six ke; fifteen minutes per ke (S7-a; the transcript prints 目周分 for 日周分). 命時起午正。午初四刻屬前日。 — the hours are reckoned from 午正, and 午初四刻 belongs to the preceding day (S7-b). RECORDED HERE ONLY TO KEEP IT SEPARATE. The fetcher flags this source with an explicit caution: it is the Huihui astronomical method as recorded in the 明史, not the Chinese civil shichen/ke system, and the two must not be merged. This dossier makes no claim that it influenced, preceded or derived from the Chinese 96-ke reforms; the ledger contains nothing that would support such a claim in either direction.

variants.label: Yuan Chong's winter-solstice row (AD 594) — recorded verbatim, deliberately not interpreted
variants.note: The Sui 開皇 14 (AD 594) submission gives 冬至：日出辰正，入申正，晝四十刻，夜六十刻 (S1-k; Siku control S2-e), consistent with the general rule 冬至晝漏四十刻，夜漏六十刻 and 春秋二分，晝夜各五十刻 (S1-b, S1-c). It then gives, in the same 冬至 row, 子、丑、亥各二刻，寅、戌各六刻，卯、酉各十三刻 (S1-l; Siku control S2-f, S2-g). THE LEDGER SUPPLIES NO COLUMN HEADING FOR THOSE FIGURES, no gloss by Yuan Chong, and no values for the remaining five branches (辰巳午未申), and this dossier declines to supply any of the three. A SECOND THING IS LEFT OPEN AND FLAGGED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED: 40 ke of daylight and a span running from 辰正 to 申正 do not sit together on the compiler's arithmetic under a 100-ke equal-chen day, and the ledger does not state what 晝 means in this table — whether it runs sunrise to sunset or dawn to dusk. The two figures are printed side by side and left unreconciled. The instrument that produced them is described: 充以短影平儀均十二辰，立表隨日影所指辰刻，以驗漏水之節 — Yuan Chong divided the twelve chen evenly on a short-shadow level instrument and set a gnomon, reading the chen and ke off where the shadow pointed, to check the clepsydra's rate (S2-h). Note that the instrument DIVIDES THE TWELVE CHEN EVENLY (均十二辰) even as the ke are being distributed unevenly (S1-j).

variants.label: When the twelve-branch hour rubric came into use — Gu Yanwu's open question
positions: EARLY — Du Yu's commentary on Zuozhuan Zhao 5, as Gu Yanwu reports it, maps the descriptive day-parts onto the twelve branches and Gu adds 一日分為十二，始見於此: the division of a day into twelve is first seen here (S9-a, S9-b, S9-c).

LATE — the 隋書 gives a five-part daylight and five lettered night-watches, 晝有朝，有禺，有中，有晡，有夕。夜有甲、乙、丙、丁、戊 (S1-d), and Gu quotes the same passage precisely for its negative: 而無十二時之目也, there was no rubric of twelve shi (S9-d). He states flatly that no Han writer called midnight 子時 and that saying otherwise is an error — 漢人未有稱夜半為子時者，誤矣 (S9-f) — and closes the whole entry by declining to answer: 未知今之所謂十二時者，自何人定之也, it is not known by whom what we now call the twelve shi were fixed (S9-e).
A DATED FLOOR FROM SCHOLARSHIP — Sôma et al.: the Suishu is the first official history in which sunrise and sunset times are described using the twelve zhi (S3-j, Tier B, cite-only).
variants.note: The 1595 山堂肆考 prints the pairing as a settled list with no commentary at all — 一日一夜總十二時，半夜子，雞鳴丑，平旦寅，日出卯，食時辰，禺中巳 / 日中午，日昳未，晡時申，日入酉，黄昏戌，人定亥 (S15-a, S15-b) — which is how the scheme looks once the question Gu reopened had stopped being asked. Both the settled list and Gu's refusal to settle it are kept.

variants.label: The hour-selection layer — TIER C DOWNSTREAM by the maintainer's brief, whatever the edition's status
variants.tier: C (downstream label). Source S13 is an imperial Siku edition and the fetcher tags it A on bibliographic grounds; its CONTENT is almanac/hour-selection doctrine, the direct ancestor of the modern 通書 / 通勝, and the maintainer's brief requires Tong Shu material to be labelled Tier C.
content: THE PREMISE — 時者，日之用也，全在幇扶日辰: the hour is the day's function, and lies entirely in supporting the day's stem and branch (S13-e). The hour is therefore not independently ruled or independently qualified; its value is relational to the day.
時破 — 時破大凶：日支衝時支也，如子日午時之類 (S13-f). The single worked example is the wu hour on a zi day; no other pair is given and none is inferred.

四大吉時 — 孟月甲丙庚壬時，仲月艮巽坤乾時，季月乙辛丁癸時 … 謂之四大吉時，又為神藏煞沒 (S13-g). NOTE THAT THESE ARE KEYED TO HEAVENLY STEMS AND THE FOUR CORNERS, NOT TO THE TWELVE BRANCHES, so they do not attach to any entry in the table above.

THE 24-DIRECTION OVERLAY — 十二支占時之中四刻，八干四維占前後時各二刻: the twelve branches occupy the middle four ke of the shi, the eight stems and four corners two ke before and after (S13-b), worked as 如巳正二刻至午初二刻屬丙方 … 午初二刻至午正二刻屬午方 (S13-c). The same note criticises practitioners who simply equate the twenty-four compass points with twenty-four hours: 術家不明天學，乃以二十四方位為二十四時，既與六壬之法不合 (S13-d).

THE MODERN COMMERCIAL FORM — a practitioner page states that there were twelve 時辰 in a day in ancient China and each makes up two Western hours (S19-a), and describes fifteen 'hour stars' with auspicious and inauspicious characters (S19-b, S19-c). The fetcher records that this page gives NO clock ranges for any of the twelve hours, so it supplies no boundary evidence at all.
variants.note: NO EFFICACY. Everything in this variant is reported as doctrine held and printed by named sources, not as a claim about outcomes. S19 is in copyright and cite-only; its snippets must not ship.

variants.label: Modern practice and the single time zone — reported without extension
variants.note: A commercial practitioner page states that the whole country runs on Beijing time as a single zone (S20-a); that when the sun is overhead in Beijing it is still in the south-east over Kashgar, about 80 minutes from its zenith (S20-b); and that the offset is 4 minutes per degree (S20-c). THE FETCHER RECORDS EXPLICITLY that the page does not state that this moves the 23:00 shichen boundary and gives no figure for hour-pillar error. This dossier reports the three statements and does not combine them into a boundary correction; that combination would be the compiler's claim, not the source's. Cite-only; must not ship verbatim.

隅中 (S9-b, Gu Yanwu) against 禺中 (S15-a, 山堂肆考) — two readings of the 巳 day-part name; both are printed in the 巳 entry.
日入者百也 in the S9 transcript, where 百 is an OCR error for 酉 (fetcher's note on S9-c) — the reason the 酉 entry does not cite S9.
日{PUA}失者未也, corrupt for 日昳者未也 (fetcher's note on S9-b) — the reason the 未 entry does not cite S9.
卜楚卜 for 卜楚丘 in the S9 transcript (fetcher's note on S9-e).
目周分一千四百四十 for 日周分一千四百四十 in the 明史 回回曆法 transcript (fetcher's note on S7-a).
己亥 for 巳亥 in the 御定月令輯要 transcript (fetcher's note on S10-a) — material, because it changes which four shi receive the ninth ke.
variants.note: The 隋書 was fetched twice, from two independent transcriptions, specifically as a control on these. That is why S1 and S2 exist as separate ledger sources and why four of the load-bearing 隋書 claims in this dossier carry a sid from each.

contestedPoints: WHERE THE FIRST DOUBLE-HOUR BEGINS. 23 hr local time as the general rule (S3-a, Tier B; S17-b, S18-a, Tier C), structurally supported at Tier A by 子正初刻當子中 (S13-a) and by an epoch reckoned 從…子正為始 (S6-b) — against the Song reckoning that began it at 0 hr (S3-b, S3-m; S17-b). Both are printed as positions; neither is chosen.

WHETHER THE DAY CHANGES AT 子初 OR 子正. The classical 夜子時 construct splits the block across the boundary, 夜子 taking only an 初刻 and 子時 only a 正刻 (S10-h, Tier A); a modern practitioner page states this as two rival schools flipping the day pillar at 23:00 and at 00:00 respectively (S18-c, S18-d, Tier C). The 1715 compilation itself lists a four-ke 夜子時 scheme among the distributions it rejects (S10-g). Three positions, none reconciled.

HOW THE HUNDRED KE WERE SHARED AMONG TWELVE SHI. At least five incompatible schemes are attested and two of them sit in the SAME 1715 compilation on facing arguments — 寅申巳亥 taking the ninth ke (S10-a) versus 辰戌丑未 taking it while 寅申巳亥 explicitly take eight (S10-b, S10-c) — beside 子午 at ten (S12-a, S10-f), 子午卯酉 at nine (S10-f), and 趙緣督's 96 large ke plus small-ke residue (S10-e). Yu Yan had already rejected two answers in the Yuan (S11-a, S11-b) and Gu Yanwu's large-ke/small-ke reconciliation is the only one that closes the arithmetic (S8-a, S8-b, S8-c). The tradition's own verdict on the dispute is printed in the same compilation: 百刻之説衆議紛紛莫有定論 (S10-d). NOT RESOLVED HERE, and a comparison view that shows one distribution as 'the' Chinese scheme misrepresents the sources.

WHETHER THE SHI IS CENTRED ON ITS 正 POINT OR BEGINS AT IT. Centred: S8-e (AD 938, 時以四刻十分為正，此自古所用也), S13-a (1741, 子正初刻當子中), and Sôma et al.'s reading of the Suishu (S3-k, S3-l). Begun: the same 938 memorial complaining the older usage had been lost and 午正 was being taken as the start (S8-f). Kept as a dispute about practice over time, not as an error to correct.

WHEN THE TWELVE-BRANCH HOUR RUBRIC CAME INTO USE. Du Yu's mapping as Gu Yanwu reports it, with 一日分為十二，始見於此 (S9-a, S9-b, S9-c) — against the 隋書's branchless five day-parts and five lettered watches (S1-d), Gu's own 而無十二時之目也 (S9-d), his flat denial that Han writers said 子時 (S9-f), and his closing refusal to name whoever fixed the scheme (S9-e). Sôma et al. add a dated floor: the Suishu is the first official history to give sunrise and sunset by the twelve zhi (S3-j). The dossier prints the question open, as Gu left it.

WHICH SEVENTEENTH-CENTURY DATE MARKS THE 96-KE CHANGEOVER. 1628 (S3-g, S17-e) against Kangxi 9 = 1670 (S6-e), with the intervening record showing the change recited as a charge in 1665 (S6-c) and re-validated by observatory trial in 1669 (S6-d). THE LEDGER NOWHERE SUPPORTS 1645 — the date this repo's round-1 shichen dossier carried — and this dossier does not carry it.

WHETHER THE 96-KE DAY IS A WESTERN IMPORT. The 明史 sets 命日為九十六刻 inside the passage on the Jesuits' arrival (S5-a, S5-b); di Serego Alighieri & Corsi call 96 ke of 15 minutes 'the Western division' (S4-a, S4-b); the 清史稿 lists it among Schall's forty-two points (S6-a). AGAINST ALL THREE STANDS THE 隋書: Liang Wudi reached 96 ke in AD 507 on the same arithmetic, and the text says so plainly (S1-f, S1-g; S2-b, S2-c; Gu Yanwu's summary S8-d). The dossier prints both and asserts no direction of influence — the ledger contains no source that argues the question, and inventing one would be exactly the failure this round exists to prevent.

WHETHER YUAN CHONG'S 冬至 PER-BRANCH FIGURES CAN BE READ AT ALL. Both transcriptions agree on 子丑亥各二刻，寅戌各六刻，卯酉各十三刻 (S1-l; S2-f, S2-g), and the same section says the ke of the twelve chen differ among themselves and differ before and after 時正 (S1-j) — yet the same table's 晝四十刻 and 日出辰正…入申正 (S1-k, S2-e) do not sit together on the compiler's arithmetic under a 100-ke equal-chen day. The ledger supplies no column heading and no definition of 晝 for this table. Recorded as an open reading, not closed in either direction.

honestLimits: WHAT THIS DOSSIER IS SHORT OF, stated where a reader will hit it. (1) TEN OF TWELVE CLOCK RANGES ARE DERIVED, NOT READ. Only 子 (S3-a, S17-b, S18-a) and 午 (S3-k, S18-b) carry a range from a retrieved page. The other ten are the compiler's arithmetic on three attested premises and are carried in a differently named field, clockRangeDerived, with the derivation stated in every entry — precisely so that a renderer cannot present them as something a source said. The two attested anchors agree with the derivation, which is the only check the ledger permits; a third anchor would be worth more than any other single fetch. (2) THE ONE APPENDIX THAT WOULD HAVE SETTLED (1) WAS NEVER OBTAINED. Sôma et al. pp. 897–904 list the twelve names with their intervals; four retrieval routes failed and the fetcher marks it the most on-point missing item. Nothing here assumes its contents. (3) NO RULER, AND THE ABSENCE IS NOT A CONFIRMED GAP. The maintainer's grid ruling settles the column; the evidence does not, because the fetcher did not search for one. Recorded as could-not-determine, not as 'no such thing exists'. (4) TIER MIX IS UNEVEN BY LAYER. The branch names, day-part names, animals, the ke arithmetic and the reform history are Tier A from Chinese primary texts in public-domain editions, several of them fetched twice as a control. The CLOCK BOUNDARIES are Tier B and C — the Tier A texts state the structure (子正 at zi's midpoint) rather than the hours. The hour-selection layer is labelled Tier C downstream by the maintainer's brief even though its source is an imperial Siku edition the fetcher tags A on bibliographic grounds; the label follows the content, and the file says so at the variant. (5) FOUR SOURCES ARE CITE-ONLY AND THEIR SNIPPETS MUST NOT SHIP: Sôma et al. 2004 (S3), di Serego Alighieri & Corsi 2020 (S4), and the three commercial practitioner pages (S18, S19, S20). Everything else is public domain and quotable, with the ground stated per source. (6) THE THINGS THIS DOSSIER DELIBERATELY DOES NOT SAY. It does not interpret Yuan Chong's per-branch figures. It does not reconcile 晝四十刻 with 辰正→申正. It does not assert a direction of influence between the Liang 507 reform and the seventeenth-century one, because no retrieved source argues the question. It does not merge the 明史's Huihui 96-ke scheme with the Chinese civil one, because the fetcher flagged them apart. It does not convert the Kashgar longitude figures into a boundary shift. It does not attach an animal to an hour. Each of those is a place a tidier table would have been produced by inventing the missing half. (7) NO EFFICACY CLAIM ANYWHERE.
